_README: Single source of truth for all site copy. Edit text here; the components read from this file. Conventions: (1) inline links in prose use markdown [text](url); (2) `icon` fields are string keys mapped to React icons in code (github | soundcloud | spotify | instagram | linkedin); (3) `href` of value 'mailto:...' opens email; (4) section keys double as DOM ids / nav targets — don't rename without updating nav. Button/tab labels (shows/releases/collective, projects/stack/experience) are intentionally NOT here — they're UI controls, not content.

paragraphs: I grew up in New Jersey splitting time between making things and performing them — two halves that never felt separate. In school I played competitive ice hockey (Ridge varsity and the NJ Rockets 16U AA) and trained formally as a musician: piano, oboe, viola, drums. What held my attention was always the building, whether the result was a song, a system, or a set.

I started producing at ten on GarageBand and moved to FL Studio two years later. Early on I made rap and hip-hop beats for local artists; then dance music reorganized how I heard everything. Now I produce and DJ as Monty (US) — warm basslines, crisp percussion, a UK- and minimal-leaning take on house and tech house — and I've opened, closed and supported touring artists in DC and New York. In 2026 that became a residency at Transmission, a first headline night in Brooklyn, and both ends of the night at Echostage.

I studied Computer Science at the University of Maryland, where I gravitated toward audio engineering, signal processing, and machine learning — including senior research on auditory signal processing at UMD's Perceptual Interfaces & Reality Lab. Today I'm a full-stack developer in Fiserv's Global Business Solutions group, building an enterprise payments developer portal and the AI tooling behind it. A lot of what I build starts with the music. Many projects I take on solve a problem I have as an artist — a setlist optimizer, audio-analysis pipelines, the tooling that runs my own workflow.

With two close friends I co-founded [PB&J Sounds](https://pbandjsounds.com), an East Coast collective and label built around underground house, and I hold a residency with [Beatprint](https://www.instagram.com/beatprint__) at Transmission DC. My investment is in the grassroots side of this scene — small rooms, real crowds, music you have to dig for — and in owning the whole stack that supports it, from the label's website to the software that prepares my sets.

Lately my focus has been making agentic AI trustworthy: at work, a governed multi-agent delivery platform where independent AI review runs before a human sees the code and a human approves every merge; at home, models on my own hardware and small fleets of agents, with the architecture written down before the code. I work for craft, rigor, and ownership — understanding something well enough to build it myself, and building it well enough to trust it on stage or in production.

Production is the work that compounds — it drives the long-term growth and the bookings that follow — so most of my creative energy lives in the studio and the next room I'm trying to play. The direction I care most about pulls both halves together: machine learning and signal processing applied to sound — deep learning, on-device and edge models, the territory companies like Dolby, Bose, and Sony work in — aimed at live performance and the tools producers use to make records. I want to build the instruments and systems that change how DJs play and how records get made. The engineering and the music were never two separate careers to me. They're one practice: the code serves the sets, and the sets inform the code.

projects.name: Prism
projects.description: A design for a box that splits a DJ's track into drums, bass, vocals and other, so the DJ can set each stem's level. No hardware exists yet.
projects.longDescription:
Prism is a design for hardware in the DJ booth. When a CDJ loads a track, Prism splits the track into four stems in the background. The design gives each stem its own encoder, or a DJM-V10 knob over MIDI.

The firmware is about 2,200 lines of C++20 with 54 unit tests. The tests use synthetic Pro DJ Link packets. No test ran against a real CDJ or a real mixer.

HTDemucs runs as an INT8 model on the CPU. I dropped the plan to run it on a Hailo-10H accelerator. The export to the Hailo format failed, and attention is 63.3% of the model's compute. On a Mac with an M4 Pro, the model splits audio at 5.79 times real time.

The audio never waits for the model. The model fills a buffer ahead of the playhead, and the audio callback reads only stems that are complete.
highlights: Status: software written, hardware not built
Measured: 5.79× real time on an M4 Pro Mac (INT8, 10 s chunks)
Measured: attention is 63.3% of HTDemucs compute (334.9 GFLOPs)
Target: stem controls live about 40 s after a track loads
Target: 1.9 ms audio round trip (calculated, not measured)
12 architecture decision records

projects.name: venture
projects.description: A Python system that runs on a schedule. It manages real money in Aave (DeFi) and Kalshi (a prediction market), with paper crypto trades beside them.
projects.longDescription:
I started venture in July 2026 and rebuilt it in October 2026. It runs a full cycle four times a day and a short check every 15 minutes, with no person at the screen. Most of the design decides what the system may do alone and what needs a human.

Rule-based code decides where the money goes. Coinbase is the main way in. The allocator converts funds to stablecoins, keeps gas in the on-chain wallet, and funds the Kalshi account toward a target. Transfers to the wallet or to Kalshi wait for my approval in the terminal app or in Telegram. Gas top-ups of $10 or less run alone.

Strategy and safety are separate. Each avenue runs its own logic and reports its own health, and an incident stops new risk. Once a week, Claude reads the history and may change only the settings of the paper crypto strategy. A change to any of the 11 locked limits stops the real-money avenues.

I operate it from a terminal app. The app shows every account and open position, and a setup wizard connects each service in order.
highlights: Rule-based code decides where the money goes
Transfers wait for approval, except gas top-ups of $10 or less
The weekly Claude review may change paper-strategy settings only
A change to a locked limit stops the real-money avenues
Paper trades run beside the real accounts
Terminal app and a setup wizard for each service

projects.name: superset
projects.description: A local tool that analyzes a DJ library and puts tracks in an order by key, tempo and energy. It reads Rekordbox XML and exports the set as JSON.
projects.longDescription:
superset puts a DJ set in order. I still choose the tracks. It reads a Rekordbox library, analyzes each track, and proposes an order that follows key and energy.

The analysis has three stages. librosa measures tempo, key, a 16-point intensity curve and spectral features. Essentia models add genre, mood, danceability and an embedding. A 4-bit Qwen2.5-3B model on MLX writes notes for each transition from those numbers. It does not hear the audio.

A greedy walk over a cost matrix makes the order. The cost weighs tempo, energy, key on the Camelot wheel, mood, spectral match and position in the set.

Everything runs on the Mac after a first download of the models. A test run on 41 tracks took 4 to 8 minutes on an M4 Pro. The public repo holds the March 2026 version (v1), which grouped tracks with KMeans and DBSCAN.
highlights: Three stages: librosa, Essentia and a local LLM on MLX
A greedy order over a cost matrix, with the Camelot wheel for key
Measured: 41 tracks in 4 to 8 min on an M4 Pro
Works offline after the first model download
React and Electron app over FastAPI, and a CLI
The public repo is v1 (March 2026). v2 is not public yet.

projects.name: realmbot
projects.description: A bot harness for a private game server, built for TypeSafe AI's Jev decision model. Jev access did not come, so every test used stand-in models.
projects.longDescription:
realmbot tests how little control a decision model can have and still help. The model picks only a tactical mode. Deterministic code owns safety, movement and every required protocol reply.

Each model call falls back to a heuristic policy on a timeout, low confidence or an outage. An action gate guards risky game actions, and a governor limits the rate and cost of model calls.

I built it for Jev's API, but access did not come. The tests used stand-ins: the heuristic, a local Qwen3-4B, a test double and a small tabular model. A 60-minute soak ran 17,997 ticks with no disconnect.

The game server is a local open-source server that I run. The project has no anti-detection code of any kind.
highlights: The model picks only a tactical mode
Heuristic fallback on a timeout, low confidence or an outage
An action gate, and a rate and cost governor
Measured: danger threshold tuned from 0.55 to 0.30 (stand-in model)
Measured: 60-minute soak, 17,997 ticks, 0 disconnects
Local open-source server. No anti-detection code.

projects.name: brodymontag.com
projects.description: This site. A three.js scene draws a laser stage, and a GLSL pass turns each 8×22 px cell into a text glyph. A CPU version in a Web Worker draws the same figures.
projects.longDescription:
One stage stays on screen across all pages. Every visitor first sees a 2D version that the CPU paints in a Web Worker. A capable device then loads the three.js version and fades to it.

GSAP ScrollTrigger is the only code that writes scroll state, so React does not render on each scroll frame. Each page has its own composition, and a page change moves the figures to the new one.

On a production build with a 6× CPU throttle, a scripted scroll holds 120 fps (p95 frame 9.3 ms, M4 Pro, 120 Hz display). The first version went live in June 2026, and the 3D stage in October 2026.
highlights: A GLSL pass: one glyph for each 8×22 px cell
A CPU version in a Web Worker paints first
GSAP is the only writer of scroll state
Figures move to the composition of each new page
Measured: 120 fps at a 6× CPU throttle (2026-10-14)
Static pages, rendered again each hour

projects.name: here comes the kicker
projects.description: 3D kickball, first in the browser with three.js and no build step, then ported to Unity 6 in C#. Pitches roll and bounce, and throw power depends on how long you hold.
projects.longDescription:
here comes the kicker started as a browser game: three.js, plain script files, no bundler. The work went into feel. Pitches roll, skip and bounce, throws get the power that you hold, and 80s-style callouts replace box scores.

In August 2026 I ported it to C# in Unity 6 in three days. The simulation runs at a fixed step with a seeded random generator, separate from the view. The port also has a camera that looks ahead of the ball. A crowd reacts to play, and the lobby is a press box above the field.

The project is paused. Avatar progression exists only as design documents. The work after commit fce6a4b has no compile check yet.
highlights: Browser version: three.js, no build step
Held-power throws, and pitches that roll, skip and bounce
Positional defense with four difficulty levels
Unity 6 port: a fixed-step sim with a seeded RNG
A camera that looks ahead, and a crowd that reacts
Avatar progression: designed, not built
projects.statusNote: Unity port done, next steps not started

projects.name: agent-forge
projects.description: One source file for each of my AI agent prompts, built into Claude Code and VS Code versions. An eval script checks the built agents, and an optional dashboard shows them as they run.
projects.longDescription:
My agents were copies in many repositories, and the copies drifted apart. agent-forge keeps one platform-neutral source for each agent. It builds the Claude Code and VS Code versions from that source.

The build is Python with one dependency, PyYAML. It fails on any placeholder that it cannot resolve. Shared instructions, such as the brief format and stack discovery, load as skills only when an agent needs them.

An eval script runs 12 checks on the built agents, for example model routing, file drift and delegations to agents that do not exist. When the Subagent Dashboard runs, agents can post events to it. The dashboard is a Next.js page with server-sent events.

Guardrails are part of the source. The agent that operates venture must ask before any financial action. I used these agents to build realmbot, Prism and venture.
highlights: One source for each agent, built for two platforms
The build fails on any unresolved placeholder
Shared blocks load on demand as skills
An eval script with 12 checks on the built agents
Measured: lazy skill pointers cut 31,538 tokens to 20,564 (−35%, 2026-06-30)
Today the same 16 agents use 25,683 tokens (2026-10-19)

projects.name: Peak_Finding_Toolbox
projects.description: A Python toolbox that finds peaks in auditory signals: ABR waves I to V, impulse responses from SOFA files, and transients in audio. A research prototype from my PIRL work.
projects.longDescription:
I wrote the toolbox during auditory signal research at UMD's Perceptual Interfaces and Reality Laboratory. An auditory brainstem response (ABR) is a small signal from the scalp after a sound. Each of its five waves needs an exact peak mark.

For ABR, the toolbox smooths the signal by its signal-to-noise ratio and looks for peaks in up to three passes. It scores I–III–V triplets against normal time windows, then finds waves II and IV between them. For SOFA and audio files it uses a fixed threshold.

I compared its Wave V picks with manual picks for 8 subjects (54 pairs). The median error was 1.15 ms, and 41% of the picks were within 0.5 ms. It is a prototype, not a clinical tool. Waves I to IV have no benchmark.

It reads EEG through MNE-BIDS, SOFA files through h5py, and audio through soundfile. I stopped work on it in May 2025.
highlights: ABR waves I to V, smoothed by the signal-to-noise ratio
Measured: Wave V median error 1.15 ms against manual picks (8 subjects)
Measured: 41% of Wave V picks within 0.5 ms
Impulse responses from SOFA files, and transients in audio
Loaders for MNE-BIDS, h5py and soundfile
A research prototype. Not clinically validated.

experience.description: Full-stack developer in Fiserv's Global Business Solutions group. I work on an enterprise payments developer portal and the AI tools for it.
highlights: I am one of two developers who lead a team of five engineers.
I proposed and built a documentation CMS (Tiptap, Yjs CRDTs, Fastify, Postgres) with versions and approvals. Two or more people can edit a page at the same time. It became the team's CMS.
I built a delivery platform for AI agents. An independent AI review runs before a human reads the code, and a human approves each merge. The team adopted it.
